newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. appeals for a cease-fire in Afghanistan.
newsitem.headline: U.N. appeals for a cease-fire in Afghanistan.

text.p: U.N. Security Council members called on Wednesday for an immediate end to the fighting in Afghanistan and for peace talks as the government denied the capital was about to fall to the Taleban militia.

The appeal was announced after a meeting of the 15-nation Security Council in New York, following a string of spectacular military successes for the radical Islamic Taleban that has brought it to the gates of Kabul.

"The members of the council call upon the parties to stop fighting immediately, to agree to a ceasefire and to enter into serious negotiations to find a political solution to this conflict," the current council president, Alfredo Lopes Cabral of Guinea-Bissau, told reporters.
The council, which has made similar appeals before without success, was particularly concerned by the humanitarian crisis and the risk of civilian casualties in any fighting for control of Kabul.
The Afghan government asked the Security Council to meet on the crisis and accused Pakistan of supporting the Taleban.
Earlier, a top U.N. official had said the radical Islamic group could be on the verge of taking Kabul, as government resistance to its onslaught seeemed to be crumbling.
But Afghan Deputy Foreign Minister Adbul Rahim Ghafoorzai told reporters in New York the government had inflicted heavy casualties on the attackers and now wanted a ceasefire.
"The Taleban have been pushed back. ... They have sustained heavy casualties. ... Apparently, there is not any obvious danger to the security of Kabul," Ghafoorzai said.
Government forces had killed 150 fighters from the militant Islamic group, wounded 500 more and destroyed 18 tanks and 12 other vehicles in the Kabul fighting, he said.

The Taleban controls more than half the central Asian country, which has been the scene of continual fighting between various Moslem and ethnic groups since Soviet troops supporting a communist government withdrew in 1989.

Emerging from the obscurity of religious schools in Pakistan two years ago, the group has been fighting to oust President Burhanuddin Rabbani's government and impose a strict Islamic order across Afghanistan.
Pakistan's U.N. Ambassador, Ahmad Kabal, denied his country was involved and said there was no serious fighting, because there was almost no resistance to the Taleban.
"What appears to be happening is that the Taleban is advancing ... on the basis of what appear to be either defections or desertions," he told reporters.
"Everybody is surprised at the manner in which the front is collapsing."
Marrack Goulding, the U.N. undersecretary-general for political affairs, told reporters earlier there was little hope of negotiations between the Taleban and Rabbani's government.

"We are getting indications ... that Kabul may be on the point of falling," said Goulding, who is in touch with U.N. officials in Kabul. He visited the country last week to try to broker negotiations that would end the conflict.
